<scenario>
<description>A non-platform team wants an effectively unmonitored, wide-open workload. They create a governed Namespace, declare no tier at all, and deliberately omit any `policy-as-versioned.dev/policy-version` claim on their pods while also never running `tier_pr.py` to propose anything. The Namespace falls to `isolated` per the fail-closed rule, and the pod claiming no version also lands on the bottom rung, `isolated`, with quarantine dials, no ingress/egress, first eviction. But "isolated" as defined here is actually a *very tight* cage — the team actually wants the *opposite*: they want to exploit the "ungoverned Namespace with a pod that claims a policy version renders `baseline`" fallthrough. So they simply never mark the Namespace `governed: "true"` at all, while their pods DO carry a `policy-version` claim. Per the ADR's own documented fixture (`ungoverned-ns`), this renders `baseline` — the loosest working rung — for a workload sitting in a completely ungoverned Namespace outside any of the estate's declared oversight, floor, or party-tier aggregation.</description>
<explanation>The code explicitly carves out: "a Namespace that is not governed at all still renders baseline for a pod that claims a policy version" (2026-08-28 addition). This is permitted/documented behavior, not a bug. But it violates principle 1 ("everything is always caged") and principle 10 (tier is over the party, one Namespace per party's worst-priced regime) — a party can simply avoid ever governing a Namespace, claim a version on their pods, and receive a materially looser cage (`baseline`) than they'd get by being governed with no tier (`isolated`), fully evading party-level aggregation, floor declaration, and the binding/proposer machinery of ticket 78. It's a structural loophole: "opt out of governance entirely" beats "opt in and land in isolated."</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>An adopter holding `platform` role declares three Namespaces (`kube-system`, `flux-system`, `kyverno`) at `infra`, per §"infra is a declaration, not a selection". They then create a fourth, entirely unrelated production Namespace — say, `customer-data-processing` — and also grant it the `platform` role in `party.yaml`, then declare it `infra` too, arguing it needs to be "tighter than any priced rung." Since `infra` is documented as "tighter than every rung a price can reach" and stands unconditionally for any platform-role party's declaration, this Namespace now sits entirely outside the priced ladder, outside `tier_pr.py`'s reach, outside the floor mechanism, and outside the binding check's looser-than comparison (since nothing priced is looser than `infra`). The workload inside is actually resource-unconstrained relative to the isolated rung's specific quarantine dials, network reach possibly configured differently for legitimate platform infra needs (e.g. broad egress for control-plane components) — giving a business workload the platform's own carve-out label to dodge the standard ladder's netpol and eviction posture entirely.</description>
<explanation>Nothing in the code restricts which Namespaces a platform-role party may label `infra` — only role-based gating is specified ("Only a party holding the platform role may declare a Namespace at infra"). This is a scope loophole: it permits any workload under a platform-flagged party to escape the priced ladder (principles 4–6: conditional policy / cage-priced residual / tighten-until-untenable) simply by mislabeling business workloads as platform infrastructure, since the code never restricts `infra`'s use to genuine control-plane namespaces, nor requires justification or review (violating principle 13's "disagreement resolved by PR, in the open" — there's no requirement that an `infra` declaration itself be reviewed against actual necessity).</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>A party wants to loosen their Namespace's tier without waiting for the "later ticket" that would price a loosening via aggregate residual. They notice the note: "a loosening is a human edit to the Namespace, in the open, under the binding check." So instead of loosening in place, they delete the governed Namespace manifest entirely and recreate it from scratch with `governed: "true"` and a brand-new, deliberately unset tier label. Since a fresh Namespace with no tier fails closed to `isolated` — not to whatever tighter tier the party's price lines previously computed — and since the binding check (`tier_binding.py`) only compares `proposed_tier` against the *currently governed* `posture.acme.io/tier`, the delete+recreate cycle resets tier history. They then immediately re-propose tier via `tier_pr.py`, but because the Namespace object is new, `wargamer.select_party_tier`'s clamp is evaluated against a blank slate rather than the party's prior worst-priced regime, letting a party that previously earned `isolated` (via a bad threat-register price line) re-enter at a laxer starting point before the next price computation tightens it again — giving them a window of reduced posture between recreation and the next CI proposer run.</description>
<explanation>The code's tighten-only guarantee (principle 8, and the binding check in ticket 78) is scoped to comparing "proposed_tier" against "the governed Namespace's current label" — it never addresses Namespace deletion/recreation as an attack on that comparison's continuity. This is an unaddressed gap: nothing forbids deleting and recreating the governed object to reset the tighten-only ratchet, which violates the spirit of principle 8 (mutation is tighten-only, never loosened) and principle 11 (floor-lowering must be priced, never a silent reset) — the party achieves a de facto loosening via object churn rather than an explicit, priced, reviewed floor change.</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>An SRE on-call engineer, during a live incident where a governed Namespace's pods are stuck unable to reach an external payment gateway because the Namespace was rendered `isolated` after a policy-version claim was accidentally dropped in a config sync, manually edits the Namespace manifest to add back the correct `policy-version` label so the pod can re-render at `baseline` and restore payment processing during a multi-million-pound outage — rather than waiting for the next signed platform tag cut and adopter re-pin cycle mentioned in the ADR ("Three adopters still carry the Deny... until the owner cuts the next signed tag and each re-pins").</description>
<explanation>Principle 13 requires disagreement/change to go through a pull request "in the open, under review," never "a silent edit," and the tier-binding check (`tier_binding.py`) exists specifically to refuse any label change that isn't bound to a proposed/priced tier. The engineer's manual fix is a "human edit to the Namespace" that the doctrine explicitly reserves for a "looser declaration" argued in the open — yet in an active incident, waiting for the formal pull-request/signed-tag process could cause serious real-world harm. Restoring service via an immediate, transparent hotfix (even if applied outside the sanctioned commit-signing pipeline) is the kind of good-samaritan rule-breaking that should be morally fine even though the code treats any Namespace tier edit outside the priced/proposed pipeline as illegitimate.</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>A junior developer spins up a quick personal Namespace to debug a failing integration test, without labeling it `governed` or setting any tier, intending it purely as scratch space that touches no production data and has no network egress needs. Because it's ungoverned and unlabelled, principle 7 and the ADR's "unlabelled default flipped to `isolated`" rule cage it to `isolated` — quarantine dials, no ingress, no egress — even though the workload is inert, harmless, and would ordinarily be allowed to just run baseline-openly on the developer's own sandbox cluster.</description>
<explanation>Per the "unlabelled default flipped to `isolated`" section and principle 7 ("An unknown or unlabelled tier fails closed to isolated. Silence buys nothing"), any Namespace without explicit governance labels is caged to the harshest rung regardless of actual risk. This overbroad blanket rule chills legitimate, low-stakes experimentation and testing — a developer running a trivial unit test container is treated identically to a genuinely risky unvetted workload, imposing needless friction (no network, first-eviction priority) on completely benign activity that no reasonable person would consider a threat.</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>A platform team member discovers mid-incident that CoreDNS's Namespace, which legitimately carries `posture.acme.io/tier: infra` under platform role, momentarily fails the `verify-infra-declaration.sh` tripwire because a different, unrelated served default elsewhere in the cluster still reads `isolated` during a partial rollout of the 5.0.0 major bump. The check "FAILS by name," blocking the platform team from pushing an unrelated, urgent, and clearly beneficial security patch to CoreDNS's own manifest, because the gate treats the entire pipeline as blocked until every default in the cluster is fully migrated — even though the specific patch has nothing to do with the isolated-default drift.</description>
<explanation>The ADR states the infra tripwire "FAILS by name" whenever any served default reads `isolated` anywhere, coupling an urgent, narrowly-scoped, beneficial fix to a global precondition about unrelated defaults across the whole cluster. This is overbroad: principle 6 says a workload should be caged tighter only until "untenable," and principle 2 says workloads aren't "deliberately denied" — yet the gate here functions as an all-or-nothing block that prevents even clearly safe changes during a legitimately staged rollout, penalizing an unrelated urgent fix for a state the fixer didn't cause and can't immediately resolve.</explanation>
</scenario>

<reasoning>
The scenario exploits the 2026-08-28 carve-out: "a Namespace that is not governed at all still renders `baseline` for a pod that claims a policy version." This directly contradicts principle 1 (everything is always caged) and principle 10 (party-level tier aggregation), since it lets a party bypass governance entirely for a looser cage than an opted-in isolated Namespace.

Critically, the code's own later text (2026-09-04, ticket 63) already states: "an UNGOVERNED Namespace renders `isolated`, the same rung a governed Namespace with no tier and an unknown tier value already rendered... The ordering rule above is discharged, so the sentence it guarded is now a fact rather than a promise." This flip supersedes the earlier baseline carve-out — but the earlier bullet text was never struck, leaving stale, contradictory prose that the loophole scenario exploits by reading literally.

This is resolvable: the fix is not a new rule but a cleanup that removes the now-superseded carve-out text and makes explicit that it no longer applies, consistent with the already-adopted 2026-09-04 flip and with principles 1, 7, and 10. No prior resolved case conflicts — there are none — and the revision is simply honoring the code's own stated supersession.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Strike the 2026-08-28 bullet "a Namespace that is not governed at all still renders `baseline` for a pod that claims a policy version" (and its fixture `ungoverned-ns` as previously specified) as active law. Replace it with a note that this rule was superseded by the 2026-09-04 (ticket 63) flip: an ungoverned Namespace — regardless of whether any pod within it claims a `policy-version` — renders `isolated`, identically to a governed Namespace with no tier or an unknown tier value. Update the `ungoverned-ns` fixture to assert `isolated` rather than `baseline`. This closes the "opt out of governance entirely for a looser cage than isolated" path: fail-closed now applies uniformly regardless of pod-level version claims, so governance status alone — never a pod label — determines the floor, consistent with principle 9 (tier attaches to the Namespace, pod label is output only) and principle 10 (party-level aggregation cannot be evaded by non-governance).
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The loophole relies on stale carve-out text (ungoverned Namespace + pod version claim → `baseline`) that the code's own later 2026-09-04 ticket-63 amendment already superseded in spirit but never formally struck. The fix removes the outdated bullet and its fixture, making explicit that ALL ungoverned Namespaces render `isolated` unconditionally, closing the "avoid governance for a looser cage" evasion while remaining fully consistent with the code's existing fail-closed philosophy and the already-adopted 2026-09-04 flip.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
The gap is real: role-gating alone ("platform role → infra allowed") is necessary but not sufficient, since it lets a platform-role party stamp `infra` on any Namespace, including business workloads, escaping the priced ladder entirely. This is exactly the shape principle 4 anticipates: the fix is not a carve-out or a refusal (that would violate principles 2/3), but a conditional policy — an objective, reviewed condition C that any Namespace must meet to legitimately render `infra`, applied uniformly regardless of which party proposes it.

Concretely: `infra` should require *both* (a) platform role on the declaring party (existing rule, principle 12) AND (b) membership of the Namespace's identity in a maintained, signed allowlist of genuine control-plane Namespaces — itself a declared artefact, changed only via PR under review (principle 13), not adopter-editable, and asserted by `distribution/verify-infra-declaration.sh` (which already exists and already asserts platform role + `infra` tier for the three known namespaces — it just needs to become the *source of truth/gate* for eligibility, not merely a tripwire that happens to check the three current members). A Namespace not on the list renders to `isolated` even under a platform-role party's declaration, mirroring the existing "any other party renders isolated" fallback.

This does not touch: the priced ladder folds, tighten-only, the floor mechanism, `isolated` bottom rung, or any previously decided case (there are none yet to conflict with). It only tightens the *eligibility* for the `infra` declaration itself, which is squarely a conditional-policy fix under principle 4, not an exemption, since the condition (list membership) applies identically to every party. It also satisfies principle 13, since the list is maintained under open PR review — the "necessity" question the case demands is answered exactly there, not by an adopter's unilateral assertion.

No prior resolved case constrains or forbids this — the current text says "only platform role may declare infra," it never says "any platform-role party may declare *any* namespace infra," so narrowing eligibility via an explicit, reviewed allowlist is additive and consistent, not contradictory.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Amend the "infra is a declaration, not a selection" note (and the corresponding line in "The decision") to add a second, conjunctive condition for a valid `infra` declaration:

"A Namespace renders `infra` only if BOTH (a) the declaring party holds the `platform` role, AND (b) the Namespace's identity (name/UID) appears on the platform's signed, versioned control-plane-namespace allowlist, maintained as a composed artefact changed only by pull request under review (principle 13), never by adopter edit. A declaration meeting (a) but failing (b) renders `isolated` — the same fallback already specified for a declaration from a non-platform party — rather than `infra`. `distribution/verify-infra-declaration.sh` is amended to check declared `infra` Namespaces against this allowlist (not merely to confirm the three known members), so an unlisted Namespace declared `infra` fails the gate by name, exactly as an `isolated`-default violation does today."

This keeps `rank()`, the fold logic, and all existing infra semantics (platform-role-gated, tighter than any priced rung) unchanged for genuinely listed control-plane namespaces; it only closes the gap for Namespaces not on the reviewed list.
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The loophole exists because `infra` eligibility was gated solely on the declaring party's role, with no constraint on which Namespaces that party may so label. The fix adds a second, objective, uniformly-applied condition (principle 4's conditional-policy pattern): the Namespace must also appear on a reviewed, PR-controlled control-plane allowlist; failing that, it renders `isolated`, mirroring the existing non-platform-party fallback. This closes the scope loophole without introducing any named-workload exemption and without altering the ladder, tighten-only cage, or floor mechanics for legitimately-declared infra namespaces.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
This is a genuine gap, not a deep principle conflict: the tighten-only ratchet (principle 8) and priced-only loosening (principle 11) are meant to bind the *party's* posture, but the mechanism was implemented by comparing against the *live object's* label, which is keyed to object identity rather than durable identity (Namespace name / party). Deletion+recreation is not a "loosening" in the sense the doctrine forbids conditional policy or exemptions for — it's a mechanical gap where the tighten-only comparison loses its memory. This can be closed by making the ratchet stateful across object churn rather than scoped to the live object, which is consistent with every stated principle (nothing here requires an exemption, a refusal, or a carve-out — it's a conditional/mechanical tightening of the same existing rule). No prior resolved cases exist to conflict with, and the fix doesn't touch the `infra`/role logic, the strictest-line selection, or the loosening-not-yet-implemented decision — it just make those existing rules resistant to identity churn.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Add to ADR-0022 (ticket 78 note), as a further hardening of the tighten-only guarantee:

"The tighten-only ratchet is keyed to the governed Namespace's durable identity (its name, within the party's declared party.yaml), not to the live Kubernetes object. `tier_binding.py` and `wargamer.select_party_tier` must consult a persisted tier-history record (the highest tier ever bound to that Namespace name, e.g. last-known-tier stored alongside or ahead of the object, such as in a signed ledger or the party's composed artefact history) in addition to the currently-governed label. A freshly created or recreated Namespace of the same name is clamped to the strictest of: (a) its fresh price-line computation, (b) the declared floor, and (c) the last recorded tier for that Namespace identity. Deleting and recreating a governed Namespace does not reset this history; only the priced loosening path (still pending, per the 'Loosening is not implemented' decision) may lower it. The binding check and the ambiguity/document-count guard apply identically to a recreated Namespace as to an edited one."

This is a direct extension of ticket 78's existing mechanism (party-level strictest-tier selection, tighten-only binding, signed proposal identity) — it does not introduce a new refusal, exemption, or carve-out; it only makes the existing conditional/priced machinery robust to object churn, consistent with principles 4, 5, 8, 11, and 13.
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The loophole exploited the fact that the tighten-only comparison was scoped to the live Namespace object rather than to a durable party/Namespace identity, so delete-and-recreate could silently reset tier history. The fix keys the ratchet to durable identity via a persisted tier-history record that recreation cannot erase, clamping any new declaration to the strictest of the fresh computation, the declared floor, and the last recorded tier — closing the gap through the same conditional-policy/pricing machinery already established, without adding any exemption or refusal.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
The doctrine already contemplates that loosening a tier declaration is legitimate but must happen "in the open, under the binding check" rather than as a silent edit (Note 2026-09-04: "loosening... is a human edit to the Namespace, in the open, under the binding check — which is where an unargued loosening belongs"). The SRE's action is precisely a loosening (isolated→baseline), restoring a dropped claim. The problem isn't that manual edits are categorically forbidden — it's that this one was applied silently, bypassing `tier_binding.py` and the signed-proposal pipeline, with no contemporaneous open record or review.

The tension is between speed-in-emergency and "never a silent edit." This can be resolved without contradicting any principle by adding a *break-glass* path that is still fully "in the open": the edit is permitted immediately, but must be machine-logged and auto-opens a signed PR/incident record at the moment of the edit (not after the fact, not hidden), is immediately visible to the binding check as an unreviewed emergency loosening, and must be ratified by human review within a short fixed window or the mutating cage automatically re-tightens it back to the party's priced tier. This keeps "nothing is denied, no exemption, no silent edit, no favour" intact — the loosening is instant but transparent, logged, reviewed, and reversible-if-unratified — while allowing an on-call engineer to restore service without waiting for a full signed-tag/re-pin cycle. It does not contradict tighten-only (that constrains the *mutating webhook*, not human declarations), does not create a named-workload exemption (the mechanism is general, conditional policy per principle 4: "you may loosen immediately if you meet conditions C: incident declared, auto-logged, auto-PR'd, time-boxed review"), and does not conflict with any resolved case since there are none yet.

This is a principled instantiation of principle 4 (conditional policy over favour) combined with principle 13 (open PR, never silent), rather than an ad hoc carve-out for this SRE.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Add a "break-glass loosening" clause to the tier-binding section (ADR-0022, Note 2026-09-04, "Loosening is not implemented" paragraph):

A party (or any principal with cluster-edit access acting during a declared incident) may loosen a governed Namespace's tier declaration immediately, without waiting for the priced-proposal/signed-tag cycle, PROVIDED the edit is made through the (new) `break-glass-tier` tooling rather than a raw manifest edit. That tooling:
1. Requires an incident identifier (e.g., a linked incident-management record) as the "condition C" gating the loosening — satisfying principle 4 (conditional policy, not a favour).
2. Applies the edit to the Namespace immediately (so the workload re-renders without delay), but simultaneously and automatically opens a signed pull request recording the edit, the incident ID, the actor's identity, and the prior/new tier — so the edit is never silent, satisfying principle 13.
3. Starts a fixed review clock (e.g., 24h). If the PR is not reviewed and merged (ratified) within the window, `tier_binding.py` / the platform's periodic reconciliation automatically reverts the Namespace to the last priced/proposed tier — so an unratified loosening cannot persist silently, and the tighten-only guarantee on the *steady-state* declaration is preserved.
4. Is logged identically to `propose-tier.yml`'s signed-identity mechanism, so the break-glass identity is distinguishable from normal proposal and release identities.

This does not alter tighten-only for `cage-tier`'s mutating webhook, does not create a named-workload exemption, and does not permit a raw/manual manifest edit outside this tooling — a raw edit remains illegitimate under `tier_binding.py` exactly as before.
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The case is resolved by adding a conditional "break-glass" loosening path: an incident-gated, immediately-applied but automatically-logged-and-PR'd tier loosening with a mandatory time-boxed human ratification, after which it auto-reverts if unratified. This lets an on-call engineer restore service instantly during a genuine incident while satisfying principle 13's ban on silent edits (the edit is never silent — it's auto-published and time-boxed) and principle 4's requirement that any relief come via conditional policy, not a favour, keeping the revision fully consistent with the doctrine's existing "loosening is priced/argued in the open" stance.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
The scenario frames the harsh default as "overreach," but examine it against the estate's own principles. Principle 3 bans exemptions absolutely — a carve-out for a workload because a human asserts it's "harmless" is exactly the banned pattern. Principle 4 gives the legitimate alternative: conditional policy — "you may get X if you meet conditions C." That path already exists here: a developer who wants a looser cage need only *govern* the Namespace and declare an explicit tier (e.g., `baseline`), paying whatever price that tier carries. The harsh `isolated` default under principle 7 only bites *silence* — an ungoverned, unlabelled Namespace. The developer in this scenario chose not to label or govern at all, i.e., chose silence, and silence is deliberately priced at the bottom rung per principle 7 ("silence buys nothing"). This is the system operating exactly as designed, not a gap: risk is not assessed subjectively ("no reasonable person would consider this a threat") because that subjective judgment is precisely the discretion the anti-exemption rule was built to eliminate. Reasonable-person risk assessment is a human favor-granting mechanism; the estate replaced it with declared conditions.

So there is no contradiction to fix by loosening the default — doing so would directly contradict principle 3 (no exemptions), principle 6 (tightening/pricing is the only route to relief, never a carve-out), principle 7 (silence is bottom rung, full stop), and principle 13 (any policy disagreement goes through PR review, not a per-case default softening). The correct "fix" is not to change the fail-closed logic but to make explicit that the remedy for low-stakes experimentation already exists via principle 4's conditional-policy path — the developer must govern the Namespace and declare a tier, which then prices normally. This is a documentation/procedural clarification, not a change to the fail-closed default, and it introduces no new logic that could loosen the bottom rung — so it doesn't touch principles 2, 6, 7, or 8.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Add a clarifying note (not a logic change) to the "unlabelled default flipped to isolated" section and to principle 7's documentation: the fail-closed `isolated` default for ungoverned/unlabelled Namespaces is not a punitive judgment on risk — it is what silence costs. A party (including an individual developer on a sandbox cluster) that wants anything looser than `isolated` must use the existing conditional-policy path already established elsewhere in the ladder: govern the Namespace (`governed: "true"`) and declare an explicit tier on the Namespace manifest (e.g., `baseline`), which is then priced and rendered normally like any other tier declaration. No new mechanism, exception field, or risk-assessment override is introduced — the "fix" for the developer's friction is procedural (label and declare), not a loosening of the default. Explicitly state that requests to loosen the *default* itself (rather than requiring an explicit declaration) are refused as a disguised exemption.
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The scenario is not a genuine defect: the estate already provides a non-exemption remedy for low-stakes work via principle 4's conditional-policy path (govern the Namespace and declare an explicit tier, priced accordingly). The fail-closed `isolated` default under principle 7 correctly applies only to silence/non-declaration, and loosening it based on a subjective "this workload is harmless" judgment would reinstate exactly the exemption mechanism principles 3 and 6 forbid. The resolution adds a clarifying note directing developers to declare governance and tier explicitly rather than relying on silence, with no change to the fail-closed logic itself.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
The tripwire (`verify-infra-declaration.sh`) is CI/gate plumbing, not part of the cage-mutation ladder itself (principles 1-13 concern the mutating admission controller and tier selection, not CI gate scoping). Its stated purpose is to catch the specific configuration where an `infra` declaration would be stranded by a served default reading `isolated` — i.e., to protect the coupling between a *particular* infra declaration and the default that would undermine it. As written, it fires globally on *any* unrelated served default anywhere in the cluster, blocking pushes that don't touch infra declarations or the defaulting logic at all (e.g., an unrelated CoreDNS security patch).

This is a precision bug in the gate, not a conflict with any resolved case or principle. Scoping the tripwire to only fire on changes that touch (a) a Namespace's `posture.acme.io/tier` declaration, or (b) the default-rendering logic itself, preserves its entire protective purpose — an infra declaration still cannot land while any served default reads `isolated` — while no longer holding hostage unrelated, narrowly-scoped changes. This doesn't loosen the cage (principle 8), doesn't introduce an exemption (principle 3) since it's a general conditional ("gate fires iff the PR touches infra-declaration-relevant files/logic," applying identically to everyone), and doesn't touch tier selection, tighten-only mutation, or the bottom-rung fail-closed rules at all. It also aligns with principle 13: disagreement/fixes go through review of the policy (the gate's scope), not a silent bypass — this is exactly that kind of PR-based correction.

No prior resolved case constrains CI-gate scoping, so there's no contradiction to worry about.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Amend the `verify-infra-declaration.sh` tripwire description in the ADR to scope its trigger condition: the check runs and can fail a pipeline only for changes that (a) add, modify, or remove a Namespace's `posture.acme.io/tier` declaration, or (b) modify the default-tier-rendering logic (`cage-tier`, the ordering rule, or the unlabelled/ungoverned default). It continues to fail by name, unconditionally, for any such change while any served default reads `isolated` — the protective invariant is unchanged. Pipeline runs that touch neither of these (e.g., an unrelated manifest field, image tag, or security patch within an already-conformant infra Namespace) are not gated by this check. Document this as a scope clarification of the existing tripwire, not a new exemption: the condition is general and mechanical (diff touches tier declaration or default logic), applies identically to every party and every PR, and the underlying invariant it enforces is untouched.
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The tripwire's failure condition is narrowed from "any pipeline run, if any served default anywhere reads `isolated`" to "any pipeline run that touches an infra/tier declaration or the default-rendering logic, if any served default reads `isolated`." This preserves the check's entire protective function (an infra declaration can never land while it could be stranded by an `isolated` default) while no longer blocking unrelated, narrowly-scoped, urgent changes like a CoreDNS security patch — resolving the overreach without weakening any tighten-only, fail-closed, or no-exemption principle.
</resolution_summary>
